theory.title: Rational and Irrational Numbers
content: A rational number can be written as p/q where q ≠ 0.
Its decimal form either terminates or repeats forever.
An irrational number cannot be written as p/q, such as √5 or π.
Together, rational and irrational numbers make up the Real Numbers.

theory.title: Laws of Exponents
content: Exponent laws simplify expressions involving powers of numbers.
For example, a^m × a^n = a^(m+n) for any real number a.
These rules help solve numerical problems efficiently.

theory.title: What is a Polynomial?
content: A polynomial is an expression with variables and coefficients.
Example: 3x² + 2x − 5 is a polynomial of degree 2.
The degree is the highest power of the variable.

theory.title: Zeroes of a Polynomial
content: A zero of a polynomial is a value of x where the polynomial equals zero.
Zeroes can be found algebraically or read off from a graph.
The Factor Theorem links zeroes directly to factors of the polynomial.

theory.title: The Cartesian Plane
content: Two perpendicular number lines, the x-axis and y-axis, form the Cartesian plane.
Their intersection point is called the origin, with coordinates (0, 0).
The plane is divided into four quadrants, numbered I to IV.

theory.title: Plotting Points
content: Every point is located by an ordered pair (x, y).
The first value (x) gives the horizontal distance, the second (y) the vertical distance.
The sign of x and y determines which quadrant a point lies in.

theory.title: Linear Equations and Their Graphs
content: A linear equation in two variables has the form ax + by + c = 0.
It has infinitely many solutions, each an ordered pair (x, y).
The graph of every solution set is always a straight line.

theory.title: Reading Solutions from a Graph
content: Any point lying on the graph of the equation is a solution to it.
Points on the axes, like (0, 0) for the x-axis and y-axis equations, are special solutions.
Graphs help verify solutions and solve real-life problems.

theory.title: Basic Geometrical Ideas
content: Euclid built geometry as a logical system from basic assumptions.
Points, lines, and planes are treated as undefined terms.
A line has infinite length in both directions but no width.

theory.title: Axioms and Postulates
content: Axioms are universally accepted truths used across all of mathematics.
Postulates are assumptions specific to geometry.
Euclid's postulates, such as extending a line indefinitely, form the basis of plane geometry.

theory.title: Angles Formed by Intersecting Lines
content: Two angles that add up to 180° are called supplementary angles.
Two angles that add up to 90° are called complementary angles.
Vertically opposite angles, formed by two intersecting lines, are always equal.

theory.title: Parallel Lines and Transversals
content: A transversal cutting two parallel lines creates predictable angle pairs.
Corresponding angles are equal, and alternate angles are equal.
The angle sum of a triangle is always 180°.

theory.title: Congruence of Triangles
content: Two triangles are congruent if they have exactly the same shape and size.
In an isosceles triangle, angles opposite the equal sides are equal.
The sum of any two sides of a triangle is always greater than the third side.

theory.title: Criteria for Congruence
content: SSS congruence compares all three sides of two triangles.
SAS congruence uses two sides and the angle between them.
ASA and RHS are two other criteria used to prove congruence.

theory.title: Properties of Parallelograms
content: A quadrilateral has four sides and four angles.
In a parallelogram, opposite sides are equal and parallel.
The sum of all interior angles of a quadrilateral is always 360°.

theory.title: Special Quadrilaterals
content: A rectangle has all angles equal to 90°.
A rhombus has all sides equal, with diagonals bisecting each other at right angles.
A square combines the properties of both a rectangle and a rhombus.

theory.title: Parts of a Circle
content: A circle is the set of all points equidistant from a fixed center.
The radius joins the center to a point on the circle; the diameter is the longest chord.
An arc is a part of the circle's circumference.

theory.title: Chords and Angles in a Circle
content: Equal chords of a circle subtend equal angles at the center.
The angle subtended by a diameter at the circle is always 90°.
These theorems simplify many geometric proofs involving circles.

theory.title: Finding Area Without Height
content: Heron's formula finds the area of a triangle using only its three side lengths.
It is especially useful for scalene triangles where the height is not known.
The formula needs the semi-perimeter, s, calculated first.

theory.title: Using the Semi-Perimeter
content: The semi-perimeter s equals (a + b + c) / 2, where a, b, c are the side lengths.
Area is then found as √(s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c)).
This method applies to real-life triangular fields and plots.

theory.title: Surface Area of Solids
content: 3D solids like cubes, cuboids, cylinders, cones, and spheres occupy space.
Surface area measures the total outer covering of a solid.
A cube with side a has total surface area 6a².

theory.title: Volume of Solids
content: Volume measures the space occupied inside a solid.
A cuboid's volume is length × breadth × height.
A sphere's volume is (4/3)πr³, where r is the radius.

theory.title: Collecting and Representing Data
content: Statistics is the branch of mathematics dealing with collection and analysis of data.
Bar graphs use rectangular bars to represent categorical data.
Histograms represent continuous class-interval data with adjoining bars.

theory.title: Interpreting Data
content: The mean is the average of all data values.
The mode is the value that occurs most frequently in a data set.
Graphs and averages together support informed decision making.
